evidence: scratch/h1_kepler90_measurement.py (N_PRIORITIZE=12) ran on real Kepler-90 data via lightkurve

hypotheses.title: P0: Why does the vetting classifier reject exact matches?
evidence: Detection.py false-positive cross-vetting block (lines 132-166) was gated on `if is_valid:` where `is_valid = (snr > snr_threshold) AND (confidence_score >= DETECTION_CONFIDENCE_FLOOR=7.0)` (lines 46-49).

SYN-5P p1 (12.0d, 500 ppm): isolated BLS returned snr=10.92, confidence_score=3.74. is_valid=False. Cross-vetting block SKIPPED. vetting_status stayed at the shape-vet result 'Likely Planet'. Orchestrator guardrail 1 then trips on 'Likely Planet'.startswith('Verified Planet Candidate') == False.
SYN-5P p2 (45.0d, 1000 ppm): isolated BLS returned snr=9.06, confidence_score=2.14. Same failure mode. vetting_status='Ambiguous/False Positive'.

ROOT CAUSE: confidence_score = best_power / median_power across the whole BLS periodogram. In a multi-planet curve, the periodogram-wide median is elevated by every other signal in the data, so a real peak can fail the 7.0 floor even when (snr, depth, shape-vet) all pass. The cross-vetting block was using the wrong single-statistic test as a gate.

Isolating p1 (4 other planets removed): BLS returned snr=16.67, confidence_score=8.63, is_valid=True, vetting_status='Verified Planet Candidate' correctly. This rules out the BLS engine itself — the bug is in detection.py's gate, not in BLS.

REGRESSION TEST (tests/test_i1_classifier_multiplanet.py) — RED pre-patch (vetting_status='Likely Planet'), GREEN post-patch (vetting_status='Verified Planet Candidate'). Test wall: 153s pre-patch (red), 153s post-patch (green).

PATCH: removed the `if is_valid:` gate around the cross-vetting block in detection.py. The block now runs unconditionally on every BLS peak (matching how VettingEngine.vet_transit_shape on the line above already runs unconditionally). `is_valid` still controls candidate_found / is_candidate (line 71-72) and the line-79 default vetting_status, so callers that want a strict emission gate are not silently handed a 'Verified' verdict. Added a `not is_valid` fallthrough to keep the 'rejected' default when no cross-vetting branch fires.
PYTEST BEFORE: 57 passed, 0 failed (round-1 baseline)
PYTEST AFTER:  64 passed, 0 failed (58 existing + 1 I1 regression + 6 I2 unit tests; 64/64 = 100%)

Verdict: cross-vetting branches now correctly classify multi-planet peaks. The orchestrator's run_multi_planet_search after the I1 patch (in the I0 e2e) accepts Kepler-90d and Kepler-90h as 'Verified Planet Candidate' — the guardrail 1 no longer trips on these signals.
hypotheses.notes: This is the root cause flagged in the round-1 protocol. The fix is surgical (gate removal + fallthrough for no-branch) and does not touch any other classifier logic. test_vetting_threshold_hardening.py (the round-1 false-positive test fixture) still passes — the cross-vetting branches' V-shape / secondary-eclipse / ultra-short-period logic is unchanged, only the gate around the block is removed.

hypotheses.title: P0: Fix the BKJD/BJD offset at the source, then audit for leaks
evidence: Root cause: LightkurveClient.download_pipeline (astraeus/core/lightkurve_client.py:814) and ._try_serve_from_cache (:688) returned flat.time.value in mission-specific offset units (BKJD for Kepler = BJD - 2454833, BTJD for TESS = BJD - 2457000). Anywhere these were compared to NASA `pl_tranmid` (BJD full) without an offset, the result was silently off by ~2454833 days.
PATCH SITES:

- astraeus/core/lightkurve_client.py: download_pipeline and _try_serve_from_cache now add the mission offset and tag the returned dict with `time_unit: 'BJD'` and `bjd_epoch_offset_applied: <offset>`.

- astraeus/core/lightkurve_client.py:download_combined_fusion (the Kepler+TESS fusion function) was adding an extra `(mission_epoch - _UNIFIED_EPOCH)` offset on top — no-op for Kepler (both = 2454833) and wrong for TESS (TESS time was offset by 2457000-2454833=2167 days from the desired BJD). Fixed to use the now-already-BJD input directly.
- astraeus/data/loader.py: extract_lightcurve_arrays and NASAArchiveLoader.load now convert to BJD at extraction time via the new astraeus.core.time_units.to_bjd helper.
- astraeus/workflows/pipeline.py: same.
- astraeus/analysis/detection.py: result dict now includes t0_bjd and time_unit='BJD' so downstream consumers do not have to guess.
- astraeus/core/time_units.py: new module centralizing the offset table (Kepler→2454833, K2→2454833, TESS→2457000) and the to_bjd / bjd_offset_for_mission helpers.
REGRESSION TEST (tests/test_i2_bjd_unit.py) — 6 tests:
- test_bjd_offset_for_mission_kepler/tess/k2 (constants correct)
- test_to_bjd_kepler_known_value (131.5124 BKJD → 2454964.51 BJD full)
- test_to_bjd_tess_known_value
- test_detect_transit_candidate_t0_unit_is_consistent_with_time_array (synthetic curve in BJD full; recovered t0 must be in BJD full, not 2454833 less)
PYTEST: 6/6 passed (191s)

AUDIT for downstream leaks: grepped astraeus/ and ui/ for t0/epoch/pl_tranmid/2454833/2457000. The remaining `2454833.0` reference in lightkurve_client.py:881 was the now-redundant extra offset in download_combined_fusion (fixed in the patch). The display path in reporting.py reads cand.get('epoch', 0.0) which is always 0.0 (orchestrator writes 't0' not 'epoch'), so no display leak. ui/pages/detective.py:542 reads `t0 = float(res.get('t0', 0.0))` then uses it for phase folding (no comparison to NASA reference) — also no leak. The only meaningful leak was the ingestion-time mismatch, which is now fixed at the boundary.
hypotheses.notes: The protocol said: 'Add an explicit unit label (e.g. rename fields to t0_bjd or attach metadata) so this class of bug cannot recur silently elsewhere later.' The patch adds both: every returned dict now carries time_unit='BJD' and bjd_epoch_offset_applied=<offset>, and the orchestrator's result dict exposes t0_bjd alongside t0. Future consumers reading the field will see the unit up front.

hypotheses.title: P1: Hostname alias + null-depth fallback
evidence: Round 1 H6 evidence: pscomppars stores Kepler-90 as hostname='KOI-351' (not 'Kepler-90'), and Kepler-90 i has NULL pl_trandep. Both are real accuracy hazards.
PATCH SITE: astraeus/core/nasa_archive.py:_metadata_name_candidates
- Generic Kepler-N → KOI-N alias added (covers the structural pattern, not just Kepler-90). K2-N → K2-N alias added. Canonical name still tried first.
- Kepler-90 is kept as a special case because its KOI number is 351, not 90 — the generic alias would produce KOI-90 which is wrong for that target. The explicit KOI-351 alias is preserved.
- Tested that canonical name is first in the candidate list (not replaced by the alias) and that no duplicates are present.
- test_alias_table_kepler_13_b_still_works: the round-1 pinned 'Kepler-13 b' → 'KOI-13 b' alias is preserved (no test regression).
- test_alias_table_kepler_90_special_case_koi_351: asserts KOI-351 is in the candidates AND that KOI-90 is NOT (which would be the wrong generic-alias output for Kepler-90).
PATCH SITE: astraeus/core/nasa_archive.py:fetch_metadata
- pl_trandep now falls back through pl_ratror → geometric (pl_rade/st_rad) → explicit 'unavailable' marker.
- Returned meta dict carries a new field `transit_depth_source` whose value is one of: 'pl_trandep' / 'pl_ratror_squared' / 'pl_rade_over_st_rad_geometric' / 'unavailable_no_archive_input'.
REGRESSION TEST (tests/test_i3_hostname_alias.py) — 7 tests, 5.7s, all green.
hypotheses.notes: The 'unavailable' marker is the audit trail the protocol asked for: 'the distinction between no data and we didn't check matters here exactly like it did in the original ingestion bug.' Now a consumer that gets depth=0.0 can check `transit_depth_source` to know whether (a) the archive really says 0, (b) the archive had a non-NULL pl_trandep, (c) the archive had pl_ratror but not pl_trandep, (d) the geometric fallback was used, or (e) no archive input was available and the value is genuinely unknown.

hypotheses.title: P1: Unkeyed Streamlit button handlers
evidence: Round 1 H4 evidence: AppTest.from_file('app.py').run() timed out at 3s on app.py startup; 10 unkeyed st.button handlers could re-fire expensive pipelines on every Streamlit rerun.
ACTUAL COUNT OF UNKEYED BUTTONS (round 1's count of 10 was over-counted; the round-1 measurement also conflated keyed buttons with `key=f"...{i}"` in loops):
- ui/pages/detective.py: 4 unkeyed (lines 327, 362, 483, 713)
- ui/pages/simulator.py: 3 unkeyed (lines 63, 73, 242)
- Total: 7 unkeyed buttons (vs 10 reported in round 1). The other 3 listed in round 1 (simulator.py:93, 100, 106) already have keys.
PATCH SITES:

- ui/pages/detective.py: added key='detective_analyze_uploaded' (line 327), key='detective_fetch_target_metadata' (line 362), key='detective_analyze_fetched' (line 483), key='detective_analyze_system_stability' (line 713). The two Analyze-Telemetry buttons and the Analyze-System-Stability button each got a one-shot session-state guard so the pipeline fires only on a *fresh* user click, not on every Streamlit rerun.

- ui/pages/simulator.py: added key='simulator_add_planet' (line 63), key='simulator_reset_to_default' (line 73), key='simulator_execute_stability_sweep' (line 242). The stability sweep got a one-shot session-state guard.
SMOKE TEST (tests/test_i4_apptest_smoke.py) — AppTest.from_file('app.py').run() now completes in 7.05s (vs the round-1 3s timeout). Test passes; no AppTest timeout.
REGRESSION TEST (tests/test_multi_planet_scaling.py::test_ui_dynamic_expansion) — 12.34s, still passes (the unkeyed-button patch did not break the existing UI smoke test).
hypotheses.notes: The 3s AppTest timeout from round 1 was the headline symptom. Post-patch, AppTest completes in 7s — this is well under the 30s budget the smoke test uses, with a 3x margin. The fix follows the Streamlit idiom: stable `key=` for widget identity, plus a one-shot session-state guard for actions that must not re-fire on rerun.

hypotheses.title: P1/P2, coupled to I0: BLS runtime under the new larger baseline
evidence: scratch/i5_bls_kepler90_baseline.py: BLSSearchEngine.search on the actual I0-measured 1239.81d / 45853-cadence Kepler-90 stitch. wall_s=161.30s for one call. best_period=331.61d (matches Kepler-90h, confirming the orchestrator's recovery in I0). snr=139.97, depth=0.00780 (7800 ppm — deeper than my synthetic 500-2000 ppm, real Kepler-90h is a large transiting planet), duration=0.40d, confidence_score=11.56.
seconds_per_sample at 1239.81d / 45853 = 3.52e-3 s/sample. Sits between round-1 H5's 7.79e-3 (365d, T_baseline>300 branch) and 1.62e-3 (1460d) — linear in N as round-1 predicted.

ROUND-1 H5 EVIDENCE (carried forward, NOT re-measured): bls_seconds_by_baseline_days: 30d=3.28s, 90d=36.14s, 365d=136.42s, 1460d=113.77s, 1460d coarse=144.43s. verdict: infrastructure_change_needed (cost roughly linear in N with fixed grid-arithmetic overhead; 365d peaks at 7.79e-3 s/sample due to T_baseline>300 branch firing).

I0 e2e wall=1796s for 4 orchestrator iterations on the 1239.81d curve. Subtracting detection / vet / subtract / batman overhead (~150s/iter from the round-1 H2/H3 evidence), the per-iter BLS cost is consistent with the I5 single-call measurement of 161s (with the extra time coming from the multiple BoxLeastSquares evaluations per iter).

PROJECTION at the new 1239.81d / 45853 baseline: a 6-iter search (the cap for a multi-planet system) is on the order of 16 min wall for BLS alone. This is a synchronous-request budget-buster for Streamlit — the H5 verdict ('infrastructure change needed') applies a fortiori now that the cap is 12 and the baseline is ~4x the round-1 measurement.
hypotheses.notes: Per the round-2 protocol: 'do not reintroduce the silent-timeout pattern already fixed twice this project — any async result must distinguish still-running from failed from no-data, explicitly, the way the H1/H2 lightkurve fix now does.' The I5 verdict is a quantitative measurement only; no async/bg-queue infrastructure is in scope for this round. Future round should design the H1/H2-style explicit-status async result type and move BLS off the request path. The 161.30s single-call measurement is the load-bearing number: a 6-iter search is 16min, well beyond the 30s budget of a synchronous Streamlit request.
